'Z160N FROM W.
ALLEN, EsQUIRE, Member of the Board of Revenue, on Deputation, To A.
YOUNG, EsQUIRE, Secretary to the Government of Bengal, FoRT WILLIAM.
Dated Cherra Poonjee, the 14th October 1858.
SIR, I HAvE the honor to report the result of the inquiries which I have made with reference to the Orders of Government, No.
116, of the 19th of January 1857, into the existing method of administering the Civil, Crininal, Revenue, and General Affairs of the Cossyah and Jynteah Hill Territory.

Mills visited Cherra Poonjee in August 1853, and bis Report on that district contains a full and complete representation of the state of affairs in these Hills at that period ; it seems necessary, therefore, to notice now only what nay have occurred since then, to explain what measures have been adopt- ed subsequent to 1853 for the improvenent of the adininistration of public affairs, and to show what has been the practical effect of those measures.
The Civil functions of the Political Agent in the Cossyah Hills, and the Command of the Sylhet Light Infantry Battalion, which had been conjointly held by Lieutenant-Colonel Lister since Feb- * No.

ruary 1835, were separated from each other by Orders* of the Most Noble the Governor of Bengal, dated the 1ith of March 1854, and the General, Civil and Political Administration of the Cossyah and Jynteah Hill Territory was transferred to an Assistant attached to the Assam Conmission, who was placed "precisely on the same footing as the " other Principal Assistants in the Province of A ssam." 4.
Mr.C.K.

Hudson, Junior Assistant Commissioner, was deputed by the Conmissioner to Cherra Poonjee, as an Oficiating Principal Assistant Com- missioner, and took charge of the district on the 10th of April 1854, from Lieu- tonant G.
Cave, who was oficiating as Political Agent during the absence of Lieutenant-Colonel Lister, who had proceeded to England on sick leave.
It appears that the Commissioner of Assam gave no instructions whatever to Mr.
Hudson, in regard to the manner in which his duties were to be conducted ; but being an Oficer of the Assam Commission, Mr.
Iudson very naturally and properly considered himself bound, in his off- cial proceedings, to follow, as much as possible, the rules, orders and prac- tice of the Assaun Courts.

No Public Notification, however, has been pub- lished, cither by the Government or the Local Authorities, regarding the transfer of this district to the jurisdiction of the Comnissioner of Assam, and tho public has never been officially informed what laws, rules and regulations are in force in this Hill Territory.

Before proceeding to mako any general remarks upon the state of affairs in these Hille, I purpose to notico the allegations and accusations con- tained in tlhc Memorials and Correspondence referred to in the 2nd para.
of the Governinent Orders, and shall endeavour to show what the facts really aro which have beon represented in such different lights by the contending 'parties.
Messrs.
Coleman, Haddan and Brownlow, and certain Calcutta Merchants, wish to make out, that Mr.
Inglis is a lawless oppressor and a monopolist, who upholds and carries on his nefarious commercial speculations by fraud and violence, whilst Mr.

Inglis stigmatizes his opponents and accusers as a noisy knot of unprincipled and reckless adventurers, who are cndeavouring to cncroach upon and ruin his long-established and legitimate trade in these Hills, by tamporing with the Hill people, with whom he has commercial dealings, and by exciting them by false and delusive promises to repudiate their lawful engagements with hirn.

When I arrived at Cherra Poonjee at the end of March 1857, I sent, from the Ofices of the Principal Assistant Commissioner at Cherra Poonjee and tho Magistrate of Sylhet, for all the cases in which Mr.
Inglis and his opponents had been concerned, and soon afterwards Messrs.
Coleman, Had- dan, Ialford Brownlow and other Gentlemen came to Cherra Poonjee to nake known their grievancos personally to me.
I have received from the Sylhet Magistrate 21 cases, and from the Cherra Court 36 cases, all of which I have very attentively examined and considered.
The gravest of the charges and conplaints made against Mr.
Inglis and the persons sup- posed to be bis dependents and partisans, are those of Messrs.
Coleman, Haddan and Rrownlow.
I shall, therefore, proceed to report upon them first.

I found that, although the offences charged by these three Gentle- men had been committed in the Cherra jurisdiction, no legal proceedings had been taken by them in the Cherra Court ; complaints had been made to the Magistrate of Sylhet, and certain inquiries had been instituted into them by that Oficer, but no final orders had been passed.

It appears that sioner and the Sylhet Magistrate entertained doubts as to whethor the placo where the offences lhad been committed, was in the Sylhet or the --- Page 5 --- (8) Hill district; this question might have been easily and immediately settled by either of the district Officers, but no decision thereon was given by either of them for more than five months.
From inquiries whioh I have made there can be no doubt, in my opinion, that the Cherra Court had jurisdiction in these cases.
When I asked Messrs.

Coleman, Haddan and Halford Brownlow, why they had not prosecuted their charges in the usual manner in the Cherra Court, they replied that they folt no confidencc in that Court, because it was under the influence of Mr.
Inglis, and they moreover stated that they did not dare to enter the Hill Territory again till they were guaranteed personal protection against Mr.
Inglis and his servants.

I pointed out to them, that it was not too late to proceed with their cases in the Cherra Court ; but they declined doing so, and statod that the inquiries nade by the Magistrate of Sylhet clearly proved their charges, and that they were willing to rest their cases on those proceedings.
They added that their witnesses were not then at hand, and that they could not afford' the expense and trouble of another prosecution.

They furthermore repre- sented, that their present object was not so much to procure tle punish- ment of the offenders, as to demonstrate and prove to the Government how great were the dificulties and dangers that beset Merchants and Traders who sought to establish commercial intercourse with these Hill people, owing to the baneful influence and illegal and violent proceedings of Mr.
Henry Inglis.
'When the matter took this turn, I forwarded all the papers of these cases to the Principal Assistant Commissioner, and instructed bim to allow Mr.
Inglis and all the other parties accused, to inspect the records, and to submit any defence or explanation they might desire to offer in regard to the statements that had been made against them.
I also directed the Principal Assistant Commissioner to take any evidence that they might be able to bring forward to rebut these grave charges.
These orders have been carefully carried out by the Principal Assistant Commissioner, and the cases are now complete enough to anable Ine to forn an opinion in regard to their merits.
The facts of Mr.
Coleman's case, as they appeared in evidonce, are as follows.

Colemaa left Sylihet on the evening of the 6th of October 1556 to procoed to Cheyla Poonjee, with the view of trading with the Cos- syals of that district; he seems to have been attended by a Moonshee, about 25 or 30 men, said to be coolies, and three or four personal servants.

Ile arrived at Kuppreya Bazaar, in the Cheyla district, on Wednesday, the 8th of October 1856, and took up lis quarters in a tent which had been --- Page 6 --- (4) pitehed not far from the place where the Bazaar is held.

In the afternoon of the following day, the Wahadadars, Bur Doloye, Berrajan, and a large number of (heyla Cossyahs, canc round the tett in a tumultuous and disrcspectful manner ; they were kept back, and eventually forced to retire by Mr.
Coleman's people.
Some slight scuffle ensued, and the Wahadadar and the Cossyahs seized and carried off' Mr.
Coleman's Cossyah servant " Sooroop".
It appears that this nan was taken to the house of the aforesaid Berrajan Ioloye, where he was kept in duress for about ten or fifteen days.
The objcct of the Wahadadars and their followers appears to have becn to annoy Mr.
Coleman, and to deter him from procoeding on to Cheyla Poonjee; Mr.
Coleman, however, went on to Cheyla, where he arrived on the following day.
He remained thero, endeavouring to transact business with the ('heyla Cossyahs till the evening of the 13th of October, when he left Cheyla Poonjee in a boat to return to Sylhet.

During the night, whilst his boat was passing down the Cheyla stream, not far from a place called Oomkhaboo, it was surrounded by a large body of armed men, apparently Bengalees, who ordered the Manjee to bring the boat to, and attempted to stop it.
The water being vory shallow, the assailants spread themselves across the stream and waded up to the boat.

Coleman being unable to oppose or elude his pursuers, who wero pressing on him in a threatening manner, the side ; he oventually made lis escape on foot, by a foot-path througl the heavy jungles, to the Sylhot Police Station of Pundooah, a distance of about 10 or 12 miles.
These are the facts in Mr.
Coleman's case which, in my opinion, have been sufficiently established by trustworthy evidence.

Inglis has impugned the veracity of the complainant and his witnesses, and has point- ed out certain discrepancios in their statemonts ; but in my judgment these discrepancies are not of much weight, and do not affect the general credi- bility of their ovidence.
There is, however, no legal evidence to connect Mr.
Inglis, or indeed his servants, with these outrages.
The Wahadadars Bur Doloye and Berrajan Doloye have been recognized as having been present when the Cossyabs assembled in a riotous and threatening manner at Mr.
Colenan's tent at Kuppreya Bazaar ; but it has been found impossible to identify, in a satisfactory manner, any of the armed ruffians who attacked Mr.

Coleman's boat at night, and forcc him to fee into the jungles; it is, however, clear that both these offences were committed in the Cheyla jurisdiction, and the Wahadudars ought, in my opinion, to be held responsible for them.
Inglis has solemnly donied that he has directly or indirectly instigated or pernitted either lis servants or any other person to attack or molest Mr.
Coleman or any other individual in this or any othor mannor, and I am inclined to accept this denial.
Iuglis could not have been aware --- Page 7 --- (5) of Mr.
Coleman's intention to visit Cheyla Poonjee, and therefore he could not havo given any orders about this matter ; but the Wahadadars of Cheyla Poonjee, who are entirely under Mr.
Inglis' influence and control, would not have dared, I think, to act in this lawless and violent manner to an Furopcan Gentleman, had they not fancied that they were acting in con- formity with Mr.
Inglis' wishes, and would receive protection from him.
Inglis has asserted that what occurred on the Cheyia stream when Mr.
Coleman was obliged to leave his boat and seek refuge in the jungles, was merely a dispute between Mr.
Coleman and two of his (Mr.
Inglis') Orange Chowkeydars, in which the former was tho aggressor.
One of these Chowkeydars, Juggernath Singh, who was summoned as a witness on the part of Mr.
Inglis, has admitted he struck Mr.
Coleman.
The defence set up by Mr.
Inglis and his servants is, in my judgment, very much wanting in probability and is not entitled to credit.
I directed the Principal Assistant Commissioner to call upon the Wahadadars of Cheyla Poonjee to explain why the outrages complained of by Messrs.
Coleman, Haddan and Brownlow had been permitted in their district, and why no exertion had been made by them to discover and bring to justice the perpetrators of them.

No satisfactory reply has been given to this requisition ; the Wahadadars have merely averred that they neither knew nor heard of these occurrences, which, they admit, they must undoubtedly have done had they taken place in their jurisdiction ; in short, they have contented themselves with denying facts which, in my opinion, have been satisfactorily proved, and which must have been within their cognizance.
The seizure and imprisonment of Mr.
Coleman's servant " Sooroop" are not denied by the Wahadadars Bur Doloye and Berrajan Doloye, the two principal defendants in this case; but they aver that when the Elders and Villagers went to Mr.
Coleman's tent at Kuppreya Bazaar on the 9th of who had assembled near Mr.
Coleman's tont, and that during the scufle that ensued, an old man was tripped up and fell down.

The Cossyahs, con- sidering this an insult to one of their village Elders, seized " Sooroop," car- riod him off to Cheyla Poonjec, and kept him for ten or twelve days in confine- ment in the house of this Berrajan Doloye, for the purpose of calling him to account for his misconduct before the village Durbar, according to the customs of the Cossyahs.
They assert that " Sooroop" was taken before the Cheyla Durbar, and released after he had executed a recognizance to conduct himself with propriety for tho futurc.

I do not credit these statements, and the very defence shows how insolent and overbearing these Wahadadars and their followers were when they presumed to seize an English Gentleman's servant in the presence of his master and imprison him for several days --- Page 8 --- (6) without trial, for merely obeying his orders and keeping off a crowd of turbulent and offensive Cossyahs who wore attempting to force their way into his master's tent.

The question regarding the venue of this case has never been decided by tlhe Principal Assistant Commissionor or the Magistrate of Sylhot ; the latter Oficer, by an Order dated the 12th of Novenber 1856, sent the rccord for orders to tho Principal Assistant Commissioner, who returned it to Sylhet with an Order dated the 27th Iden, to the effect that it had not been proved that the offences had been committed in the Cherra district ; and that the Sylhet Magistrate might dispose of tho case himself, or make a reference on the subject to the Sudder Nizamut Adawlut under Section 2 of Regulation VIII.
No reference, however, had becn made on the 14th of April 1857, when the proceedings were forwarded to this ofico.
I will now notice the proceedings of the Cherra Court in this case of Mr.
Coleman, which appear to have given much dissatisfaction to that Gentleman and othors.

Coleman made known his complaints to the Principal Assist- ant Commissioner at Cherra Poonjee in eight English letters, numbered from 2 to 9 consecutively ; somo of these were dispatched from Kuppreya Bazaar and Cheyla Poonjee, but the letter-carriers are said to have been intercepted, and all these letters reached the Principal Assistant Commis- sioner at Cherra under one cover on the 17th of *Dated October 18th October 1856.
On these letters the following Orders* 1856, have becn recorded by Mr.
Principal Assistant Com- missioner Hudson :-- " Mr.
Coleman's letters, Nos.
2 to 9 inclusive, were received yesterday, " addressed to me under one cover.
Coleman should, however, have adopt- " ed the usual course of submitting his complaints for investigation by " petition in my Court, in which form alone they can be attended to.
A copy " of a Bengali Durkhast, filed by Mr.
Coleman at the Pundooah Police " Pharee of the Sylhet jurisdiction, having been received from the Magistrate " of Syllhet, with a request for my co-operation in suppressing affrays between " Mr.
Inglis and Mr.

Coleman's people in my jurisdiction, the Police Darogah " of this station was yesterday ordered to proceed to the Cheyla Poonjee " district and disperse any pcople assembled there or in the vicinity, either " on the side of Mr.
Inglis or Mr.
Coleman, who appears, from some Petitions, "&c., fled in my Court ou the part of the Cossyah Wahadadars and " Zumeendars of Cheyla Poonjee and Mr.
Inglis, to have lately taken a Mr.
" Brownlow and a large posse of armed people to that place with him.

As "the Wahadadars of Cheyla Poonjee conduct the affairs of their district --- Page 9 --- (7) " themselves, subject merely, as a dependent Cossyah State, to the Political "control of this Government, and they are responsible for any breaches " of the peace that may occur there, foreigners (either Europeans or Ben.

"likely to cause disturbances and dissensions amongst their people, without " obtaining their consent, or express authority from the Officers of Govern- " ment, and proper orders have, therefore, been passed on this subject also.
" A copy of this Order is to be sent to Mr.
Coleman for his infor- " mation with advertence to his letters above alluded to.
On the 17th of October 1856,* on information received from the Sylhet Magistrate, the Cheyla Wahadadars and Mr.
Inglis, Mr.
* Appendix No.
Principal Assistant Commissioner Hudson had ordered the Cherra Poonjee Police Darogah to proceed to Cheyla Poonjee to keep the peace, and had ordered a Notificationt to be published in + Appondix No.

Cheyla Poonjee, that "aliens are in future prohibited " from proceeding into the Cheyla district accompanied by large gangs of " the authority of Government and with the consent of the Wahadadars." This Notification was submitted for the orders of the Ageut to the Go- vernor General on the North East Frontier, who approved and sanctioned it by a Proceeding under date the 24th of October 1856.
On the 3lst of October 1856,* the Principal Assistant Commis- sioner at Cherra Poonjee, with the view of preserving *Appendix No.

the peace in Cheyla Poonjee, passed another Order, pro- hibiting "any European or Bengalee aliens," either arined or collected in large parties, from entering that district for the purpose of trade, " or with any other intent," without having first obtained the consent of the Wahadadars.
To thcese two Proceedings of the Principal Assistant Commis- sioner, datcd respectivoly the 17th and 3lst of October, the Memorialists have urged strong, and I think, rather reasonable objections.
They represent that the Principal Assistant Commissioner has prematurely assumed, without any inquiry, that Mr.
Inglis was in the right and they in the wrong, and that the effect of these Ordcrs will be to give and confirm to Mr.
Inglis a close monopoly of the trade of the Chcyla district 25.

After a careful consideration of all the circumstances of the case, it scems to me that these Orders are not judicious ; they are not, I am satis- fied, necessary for the preservation of the peace, and we are under no moral or political obligation to uphold the authority of the Wahadadars against the wishes, and, I may add, the rights of the people in a matter of this kind.
The present Wahadadars are notoriously the creatures of Mr.
lnglis, and if no person be allowed to enter the district without their permission, it is very clear that the trade of Cheyla will be virtually closed against every trader but Mr.
Inglis and lis dependents.

--- Page 10 --- (8) 26.I am of opinion that these ohnoxious prohibitory Orders should be entirely and inmediately rescinded, and that full freedom of trade should be r'stored to the inhabitants of the Cheyla district.

If the present Wahadadars cannot or will not perform their official duties with uprightness and impartiality, the Cheyla community ought to be permitted to elect others, in conformity with the ancient customs of their country.
The facts which seem to me to be proved in the case of Mr.
Haddan and Mr.
Halford Brownlow are as follows.
Haddan, who had been engaged by Messrs.

Gladstone, Wyllie nnd Co., of Calcutta, to visit and obtain information regarding the Petroleum Wells in Assam and these Hilly Tracts, left Chattuck, by water, on the night of the 16th of Oetober 1856, accompanied by Mr.
Halford Brown- low, to inspect a Petroleum well which was said to be somewhere in the vici- nity of the village of Cheyla.
They travelled in a small dinghy, which was worked by two boatmen, and were attended by one personal servant.
About 8 A.

on the 17th of October 1856, when their boat had arrived at about two reaches below Kuppreya Bazaar, and not far from Katta Ghaut, its further advanco was opposed by two elephants and a large gang of Club- men, baving the appearance of Bengallee "lattials"; these men hailed the Manjee and ordered him to stop and bring the boat to the river side.
When this mandate received no attention, the Clubmen sproad themselves across the shallow water, and forcibly prevented the boat from proceeding any fur- ther up the stream towards Cheyla Poonjee.
There was a respoctably clad native mounted on an elephant, who appeared to be dirccting the movements of the Clubmen.
Whilst Messrs.
Haddan and Brownlow were parleying with their assailants, some of them made a rush upon the Gentlemon, and succeeded in wresting a gun from Mr.
Haddan's hands.

The Clubmen then seized, beat, and otherwise maltreated these Gentlemen, dragging them through the water to a single pole tent which was pitched on thc Rivor-bank, and in which they were detained in their wet and bloody clothes without food till about G r.
M., when they were conveyed in a small boat to Chattuck, and placed on board Mr.
Haddan's budgerow there, about 10 .
Messrs.
Haddan and Brownlow have asserted that their boat was property valued at about 20o Rupees.
The evidence does not show whether any property was plundered ; but the facts above stated appear to me to have becn satisfactorily established.

These Gentlemen were strangers in that part of the country, and had with them only one servant and two boatmen, who were equally unac- quainted with the people und the country, and in consequence it has been found impracticable to identify satisfactorily the rufians who perpetrated this disgraceful outrage; but the inquiry of the Cherra Poonjee Police Darogal
